title: The Fulfillment of the Covenant
english: of those in heaven and on earth and under the earth and of every tongue confessing what the Lord Jesus Christ does for the glory of God the Father. The cross bears as a symbol this exaltation. And all these things shall be spoken concerning the happening of the Word made flesh. For if even he himself happens to be [one of them], yet according to the thought it will not fit the things set forth to his incarnate presence.

And a little before, we set down as a known tradition those psalms which are written after the Alleluia among those arranged previously, and here from Psalm 150 to Psalm 178 the Alleluia is written; none of these is of a different character. Since the righteous one of David is not written [on them], it is necessary according to his tradition to [include] all the following until 178. And let this be a general observation upon all the unwritten psalms. And the saint, about to proclaim the things having happened concerning the salvation of all by the Lord, pre-announces the voices set forth. And everyone confesses with all his heart, and he alone who has loved God with all his heart, soul, and mind; and, having turned away all his loving power toward God, he loves God with all his heart; and, having consumed all his hymnographic and eucharistic power toward God, he confesses to him with all his heart in the assembly of the important ones, not in a random place or with random people. It is possible to read 'With all his heart' as follows: 'In the counsel of the upright and in the assembly, the great works of the Lord' (Ps 110:2).

Generally and broadly called the will of the Lord, the things concerning his works in part are his individual wills. If not all things he willed, he did; the creation extends broadly to his will, the individual works being fitted to the specific wills. Therefore, since the Creator is great, his works are also great, most accurately fitted to the harmony of his wills; for they do not happen as they chance, but they happen as having been sought out for all the wills. Therefore, of the works having been sought out, let no one say 'to what purpose?' For all things were created for their need; therefore, all the works of God are very good. If, indeed, the works of God are taken...

Since things happening paradoxically and marvelously (some through Moses and the prophets, others through Jesus our savior) are spoken of, the preceding words are also spoken of these. For the resurrections of the dead, the cleansings of lepers, the sight of the blind, and things similar to these, Jesus performs symbolically through them, manifesting the healings of his own humanity, which are always previously the will of God.

And if one calls virtues the will of God because he will do all my wills, he will say great works have been sought out for all the wills of God, namely the activities according to virtue. Ps 110:5,6: And indeed he gives food without exception to those fearing him with a certain paradoxicalness, just as Daniel found the best in the lion's den in Babylon; from Jerusalem, the transport of Habakkuk was brought to Babylon, carrying food to Daniel. But also, having commanded the ravens to bring bread in the morning and meat in the evening to Elijah (during a time of much famine), he nourished him who feared the Lord.

And of his old covenant, when the time of correction having been given, the end is taking up, he shall be remembered for an eternity during the age of the new covenant according to the gospel, which remains without a successor. Therefore also, to the people, he appropriated his own blood; through the bath of regeneration and the renewal of the spirit, Jesus gives the power of his works, making manifest to them what power he has commanded them to work, the people, and the words of the things that have happened. His covenant shall be remembered for an eternity.

He who partial hardening happened to Israel, the fullness of the nations has entered into salvation. But since God is good, not being satisfied with only the fullness of the nations entering into the pure and glorified inheritance, he is remembered for an eternity of the covenant toward the sons of Israel through their fathers. He will announce to the Israelite people the power he made his works, so that, having seen the power of the economy, they also might be saved, after the fullness of the nations has entered, receiving from God the inheritance appropriated and confirmed to the nations. Ps 110:7,8: Many of the divine sayings...
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The Judgment as Rectitude and the Fear of God
english: When calling the Father, we find the Lord, as 'The high hand has done all these things' (Ps 118:74). For the Word—through whom all things were made and in whom all things exist, which the Father made—is His hand creating the all. But also in a strong hand, having brought the people out of Egypt, God accomplished this in the same Son, as one of the apostles writes: 'Jesus, having saved a people once out of Egypt, twice destroyed those who did not believe' (Heb 12:26).

And since other scriptures also say that God has made all things by one hand, such as the one saying 'The heavens are the works of your hands' (Ps 89:11), and the one announcing 'The hands did not create all the host of heaven' (Isa 48:7) (this is consistent with the one who said 'Your hands made me and fashioned me' [Ps 139:13]), someone might rightly seek and find the Holy Spirit being called the hand of God; from which it is shown that the Holy Spirit is creative, in the Son and Holy Spirit of the Father, having worked the heavens and having created the host of heaven.

Among these works of the hand of God in all the saints, truth and judgment are found, happening to be truth. For He gives through the Holy Spirit a practical power, and judgment is that which judges and, with examination, defines, so that one must choose good and flee evil; but truth is what Christ gives through the Holy Spirit, namely a word of wisdom and a word of knowledge. The knowledge of truth and moral virtue are works of the hands of God, being truth and judgment; therefore, following this, all His commandments were brought forth, not spoken so as to be believed merely, but because of the immovable and certain, as it is written, 'I will give you an eternal covenant, the faithful things of David' (2 Sam 7:16).

These faithful commandments stand for ever and ever because they are of God and cannot be overturned. Concerning them, indeed, the Savior says, 'Heaven and earth will pass away, but my words will never pass away' (Matt 24:35). But do not err by thinking that the things set forth concern the commandments which are according to the shadow. For those passed away until a time of correction was given. For concerning the spiritual laws according to Him, it is necessary to hear the things set forth, as the coming thing teaches thus: 'Having been made in truth and rectitude.'

For they become understood in truth according to the doctrine of godliness. But they are also completed in rectitude with the best of guarding, as the work of the hands of the Lord, and these being found to be being accomplished in each godliness, [are] truth and judgment. But take hold of judgment for the sake of rectitude, to direct the soul toward practical and ethical virtue, and [judgment is] to be critical of things to be done and not to be done.

As God sent redemption to his people (Ps 110:9ab: He has sent redemption to his people; there is nothing else to the one saying), the Son of Man came to give his soul as a ransom for many. By the same precious grace of God, having tasted every death, we were redeemed from our ancestral vain conduct. For Christ has become to us as wisdom and righteousness and sanctification from God, and also as redemption, saying, 'I was sent to proclaim liberty to the captives' (Luke 4:18). For the redeemer and benefactor of all has released from captivity those held by the devil and by wickedness, forgiving the sins and impieties of those fleeing to him. But his goodness was not satisfied with merely redeeming the captives and their heirs, those of his own father, but he set them as co-heirs of himself, having enjoined upon them an eternal testament, so that possessing it with brevity and perfect readiness, they might receive an immortal inheritance according to the eternal and incorruptible promises.

His name, he says, is holy to the saints, but fearful to the unholy (Ps 110:9c). For just as the fountain of holiness makes those participating in it become saints, so it is fearful to those who sin by bearing it.

As the doing of righteous things is the beginning of the good way (for this is the contemplation of truth) (Ps 110:10), so the fear of God is the same beginning and introduction into the wisdom of God, which is called the same as the contemplation of truth, which to the practically righteous belongs. For as the doing of righteous things leads toward the good way, so this fear of God leads toward wisdom. The name 'beginning' can be here, not instead of an introduction, but as being a cause, since the fear of God is that which is called the cause and the beginning. And the struggle with this wisdom is understanding.
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: Divine Authority and the Virginity of Mary
english: Goodness is not for those who have merely thought about doing it, but for those who are actually doing it. For those who practice understanding, no benefit will be other than that of virtue, from whose benefit they learn the goodness of it.

Regarding all that has been theologized in the present Psalm, it is said that the end of it is that his understanding remains. For this is a fitting end for those who theologize: to say that his understanding (clearly of the one theologized about) remains forever. Since the one being praised is immortal, it is necessary that his understanding also be without end, as it lasts for all the ages.

He who does not act for the sake of anything else, but through human glory, or to avoid falling into the punishment that entices sinners, or for reward, but by choosing and acting for the sake of the good itself—for such a one will truly be blessed (Ps 111:1bc). The seed of the blessed man, who has the fear of the Lord, sows into the good land, his diligent and beautiful heart; it is possible for him to bring forth a hundredfold fruit (Ps 111:2,3). For those sowing the seeds of evils sow into the flesh, which is their weak and earthly existence (and so they reap corruption from the flesh), but those sowing into the Spirit, the powerful seed, they sow and reap into eternal life. For each of the imperfect and sinful, the Word commands: Sow for yourselves into righteousness, reap for yourselves into the fruit of life. Glory and wealth in his cosmos.

He who has heard the words of Jesus and turned them into works builds his house upon the rock, laying down the foundations of his theoretical and practical life upon the unshakable Word of God. Each one who fears the Lord has built such a house upon having willed to do what is in the commands of the Lord (that is, to have intensely willed the words of Jesus), filling it with the glory of the notions of truth and the wealth composed of every word, every knowledge, and every working good. Thus, the promise of his righteousness extends into the age of ages. Such imperfect houses they have built for themselves, having feared the Lord, so that they might not dwell in the [er...]
They wander halfway according to Isaiah, but they dwell according to the formed Jacob as a house. Others have also taken the things set forth according to the literal sense.

And the words ought not to be regarded as human. For the words of the stewards are not believed, as they are said. For indeed, one has been placed in advance by prophecy from God, Amos, who became upon the uncircumcised, and Solomon, stripping the matter bare: 'My words,' he says, 'if they are said by God.' Careless also is the divine Gospel, sometimes regarding the giver and sometimes the ministers; from the ministers he says, as Paul says, 'My Gospel,' but from the one handing it over, Paul again says, 'Just as we were approved by God to be believed to have the Gospel,' and 'That [they are] set apart for the Gospel of God'; and this is not a wonder. For it is the Holy Spirit that fills the holy men with divine things, sometimes of God and sometimes of those possessing [it], as it is said in [Luke] 'The Spirit of the Lord has rested upon him,' and 'In Spirit and in Power' [Acts].

But do not think because it is said chronologically, 'Until he goes against his enemies, he is not shaken,' that what is shaken after the destruction of the enemies is [not the same]. For how could he be moved, the one who, having the enemies removed, did not suffer this while threatening and looming over them? For it is customary in the Scripture to use such a way in many places; for regarding Mary, the Gospel says she remained a virgin until she bore her firstborn son, and so on. Since it is proper to show that the birth of Jesus came from a virgin without marriage, it is fitting that she was once in doubt. Did the virgin not undergo corruption? He says also 'she conceived'; having gone around this doubt, he says she remained a virgin until the childbirth. For if it is not said that a virgin remains until she bears, a virgin did not conceive from a man, nor did a virgin bring forth a child without [conception]. By this thought, 'I am, I am' is said by God, and 'as you may be reproached, I am.'

He says, 'God is [my] horn.' For all the righteous say this, being confident: 'In you we horn our enemies.' And he who therefore blesses his enemies in the Lord, having horned his horn against them...
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.
